The core principle is the relaxation of strict workload assignment between fast and slow nodes [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that 'strict assignment to slow and fast node can be relieved' to improve visual quality by replacing image warping with raycasting. It further details methods for this distribution, such as using a quality map to identify badly reconstructed pixels (disocclusions) and replacing them with raycasting, and using a parameter 'm' to determine when to switch from warping to raycasting based on empty layers. This directly supports the claim that the core principle involves relaxing strict workload assignment between fast and slow nodes.
supported

Unlike separation planes which create perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading approximation and poor adaptation to scene interest, flexible schemes adapt to focus regions, segmentations, or depth importance [S1].

The claim is explicitly supported by the text in Source [S1]. The passage states: 'When using such a separation plane or region to divide forward from backward sampled areas, this approach often leads to a perceivable boundary. This is mainly due to the fact that the deferred shading from warped images is only an approximation... Moreover, these regions do not adapt well to what is really interesting in a scene: often there are focus regions, segmentations or magic lenses... To account for these facts, a more flexible workload distribution...' This directly aligns with the claim that separation planes create perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading approximation and poor adaptation to scene interest, while flexible schemes adapt to focus regions, segmentations, or depth importance.

The parameter $m$ helps steer the quality vs. performance tradeoff [S1].

The claim is explicitly supported by the text in Source [S1]. The notes section states: 'The parameter m helps steer the quality vs. performance tradeoff.' The passages section confirms this with the sentence: 'Nevertheless, the m parameter can be used to roughly steer the quality vs. performance tradeoff.' Additionally, the text explains that a lower m switches to raycasting more frequently, which directly relates to the tradeoff between quality (raycasting is higher quality) and performance (raycasting is slower).

Advanced Workload Distribution Schemes are methods that distribute rendering workload between a fast GPU (performing raycasting or image warping) and a slow GPU (performing raycasting) to improve visual quality beyond strict node assignment by replacing some image warping with raycasting [S1].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. The source explicitly describes methods that distribute workload between a fast GPU (using image warping) and a slow GPU (using raycasting) to improve visual quality beyond strict node assignment by replacing some image warping with raycasting. It details the mechanism of using a quality map to identify disoccluded pixels (often caused by undersampling or holes in layered warping) and replacing them with high-quality raycasting on the fast node. All specific details mentioned in the claim (fast GPU performing raycasting/image warping, slow GPU performing raycasting, replacing warping with raycasting, improving quality beyond strict assignment) are present in the provided text.

The method addresses the limitations of traditional parallel raycasting algorithms that divide workload by separation planes in screen space or object space (sort-first or sort-last), which often lead to perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading from warped images being only an approximation to per-sample phong shading [S1].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. The source explicitly states that traditional parallel raycasting algorithms using separation planes (screen or object space) 'often lead to a perceivable boundary' because 'deferred shading from warped images is only an approximation to a per-sample phong shading.' It further explains that the method in question addresses these limitations by using flexible schemes (like quality maps based on disocclusions) instead of fixed separation planes.
supported

Distribution by Quality Maps is a workload distribution method that uses a quality map to identify badly reconstructed pixels (mostly from disocclusions or undersampling during image warping) and replaces them with high-quality raycasting [S1].

The claim states that 'Distribution by Quality Maps' is a workload distribution method that uses a quality map to identify badly reconstructed pixels (mostly from disocclusions or undersampling during image warping) and replaces them with high-quality raycasting. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section 5.2: 'Badly reconstructed pixels, which mostly come from disocclusions or undersampling during image warping, can be discarded and replaced by a high-quality raycasting.' It further explains that this is done by creating a quality map where low-quality regions (disocclusions) are filled by raycasting. The notes also confirm this definition. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
